# Overview: A multi-timescale, neuromodulated, circuit-level learning theory

Modern theories of how biological neurons learn converge on a multi-timescale view in which precise spike timing and correlated activity shape synapses via local biochemical rules, neuromodulators provide supervisory “tags” that license long-term modifications, and homeostatic mechanisms keep networks biologically viable while learning proceeds. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">At the core are spike-timing–dependent plasticity (STDP) and related Hebbian rules that capture associative learning from temporally structured inputs</cite>, <cite id="0634f1b9-1">but purely Hebbian algorithms are intrinsically unstable without stabilizing negative feedback</cite>, so <cite id="0634f1b9-1">homeostatic plasticity evolved to regulate firing rates and synaptic strength</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">Neuromodulators (acetylcholine, monoamines, histamine, neuropeptides, hormones) tune plasticity, potentially providing global supervision for otherwise unsupervised rules like STDP</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-0">At longer timescales, activity-dependent transcription (CREB/IEGs), excitability changes, and spine clustering select and consolidate synaptic engrams in neuronal ensembles</cite>. <cite id="0f6daaad-0">Computationally, BCM-style rules and dendritic processing implement objectives akin to PCA/CCA with homeostatic constraints, tying synaptic modifications to variance and correlation maximization</cite>.

# Synaptic plasticity rules and temporal coding

Modern synaptic learning is driven by spike timing and correlated firing rather than only firing rates. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">STDP strengthens synapses when presynaptic spikes precede postsynaptic spikes and weakens them otherwise, enabling sequence learning and precise temporal coding</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-2">Experiments and theory link STDP to cortical map development, receptive-field sharpening, working memory, and associative learning, while emphasizing that it rarely acts alone</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-1">Some STDP variants can stabilize postsynaptic firing below critical frequencies, but in densely connected networks rapid runaway growth can require complementary homeostatic mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-1">In this sense, STDP provides a local, unsupervised learning signal, whereas neuromodulators provide regulatory or supervisory signals that determine whether changes are stored long term</cite>.

# Neuromodulatory tagging and long-term engram formation

A central advance is the integration of synaptic plasticity with neuromodulatory “tagging” that licenses durable modifications. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">Acetylcholine modulates NMDA receptor function and thereby plasticity, and neuromodulation of STDP extends beyond classical transmitters to neuropeptides, hormones, and immunological agents</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">Neuromodulatory control can provide global supervision to unsupervised rules, helping determine which plasticity events are committed to long-term memory</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-0">During encoding, synchronized sparse activity recruits neurons into engram cell ensembles; these neurons show prior connectivity and excitability that facilitate recruitment</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-0">Spine proximity and clustering, dendritic calcium/depolarization spikes, and enhanced CREB signaling prime neurons for recruitment, linking structural plasticity and transcriptional programs to engram selection</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-0">CREB-driven immediate early genes (IEGs) facilitate LTP and engram-specific increases in excitatory transmission in hippocampus, amygdala, and prefrontal cortex during consolidation</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-2">Converging evidence shows neurons activated and neurons expressing IEGs during learning/retrieval exhibit higher firing probability and altered synaptic plasticity, and that CREB levels mark neurons favored to enter a memory trace, effectively implementing a molecular selection mechanism</cite>.

# Stability and homeostasis: keeping learning within biological bounds

Instability is a key concern: purely Hebbian feedback can drive synapses to diverge or collapse and neurons to become either insensitive or hyperexcitable. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">Hebbian algorithms are intrinsically unstable because correlated firing leads to strengthening, which further increases correlated firing</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-1">Homeostatic plasticity discovered in the mid-1990s provides negative feedback that keeps postsynaptic activity near viable ranges, preventing neurons from becoming non-firable or overly sensitive</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-1">Even with STDP’s partial stabilization, explicit homeostatic mechanisms are often needed to counter rapid rate increases in highly connected networks</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-1">Quantitatively and mechanistically, links between STDP, BCM rules, and homeostatic scaling have been developed, including energy-energetic constraints that tie firing, membrane potential, and plasticity</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-2">Complementary forms of homeostatic plasticity—scaling total synaptic strength, activity-dependent intrinsic excitability, or history-dependent synaptic availability—coordinate with STDP to maintain circuit stability during development and learning</cite>.

# Computational perspective: objectives, competition, and coding

Modern theory also connects plasticity to explicit computational objectives. <cite id="0f6daaad-0">BCM theory provides a sliding-threshold rule that implements Hebbian plasticity constrained by postsynaptic activity, with dendritic compartments adding correlations across inputs; in two-compartment neurons, the learning rule corresponds to maximizing second-order moments and correlations while implementing PCA-like and CCA-like learning under homeostatic constraints</cite>. <cite id="0f6daaad-0">Somatic-only neurons perform PCA-like learning; dual-compartment neurons perform dual learning across compartments, with the objective weighted by a homeostatic parameter</cite>. <cite id="0f6daaad-1">BCM remains a leading unsupervised cortical plasticity model, with links to calcium dynamics and to STDP for spike-based learning; soft-bound (weight-dependent) plasticity—less LTP for strong synapses and roughly linear LTD percentage for weak synapses—naturally reproduces observed weight distributions and avoids unbounded growth</cite>. <cite id="0f6daaad-2">In network models, BCM-like excitatory plasticity with sliding thresholds and pruning implements competitive learning and stimulus selectivity, while homeostatic inhibitory plasticity stabilizes target firing rates, capturing balanced competition between excitatory and inhibitory inputs</cite>.

# Dendritic nonlinearities and spine structural plasticity

Learning is not confined to the soma: dendrites integrate inputs nonlinearly and remodel synapses to implement cell- and compartment-specific transformations. <cite id="0f6daaad-0">Dendritic activity supports LTP generated by coincident proximal and distal inputs, and BCM-like rules generalize to dendritic compartments, yielding dual PCA/CCA learning when somatic and dendritic inputs are integrated</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-0">Spine clustering near preexisting spines induces local dendritic calcium and depolarization, enhancing excitability to promote recruitment into engrams, while CREB signaling and IEGs support consolidation and engram-specific synaptic potentiation</cite>. Together these mechanisms allow neurons to compute correlations and mixtures of features at different spatial scales while maintaining energy-constrained dynamics and selective receptive fields.

# From single-cell rules to circuits and systems

Modern theories explain learning as emergent from interacting synaptic, cellular, and circuit mechanisms. <cite id="0634f1b9-2">Unless synaptic changes are coordinated across synapses and neuronal properties, stability and functionality degrade; thus homeostatic and developmental constraints partner with STDP to shape maps, receptive fields, working memory, and associative learning</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-0">Synchronized sparse recruitment, CREB/IEG-dependent consolidation, and spine remodeling select engram cell ensembles that encode specific experiences</cite>. <cite id="0f6daaad-0">At the computational system level, BCM-like and dendritic learning rules implement dimensionality reduction and correlation alignment objectives, enabling neurons to extract principal components, canonical correlations, and selective receptive fields under homeostatic constraints</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-1">Neuromodulatory control bridges local spike timing events to global supervision over days to weeks, aligning synaptic tagging with energy and neuroenergetic limits, and providing a framework to reconcile short-term plasticity with long-term memory storage</cite>.

# Open frontiers and integrative principles

Two intertwined challenges define “modern” progress. First, supervisory mechanisms: <cite id="0634f1b9-0">neuromodulatory control of STDP, spanning classic transmitters and peptides, likely gates whether transient spike-timing events become durable engrams, but the precise rules and timescales across systems remain under active study</cite>. Second, stability-energy coupling: <cite id="0634f1b9-1">homeostatic plasticity, energy supply, and firing rates are deeply intertwined, suggesting a thermodynamic view in which synaptic modification must respect mitochondrial constraints and network energetics</cite>. On the computational side, <cite id="0f6daaad-1">weight-dependent plasticity and soft bounds can stabilize distributions without explicit global normalization, linking microscopic calcium- and spike-based rules to macroscopic selectivity and robustness</cite>. Finally, engram selection integrates molecular and structural plasticity: <cite id="495966f1-0">CREB/IEG signaling modulates excitability and promotes spine clustering that increases local dendritic calcium, coupling transcriptional programs to synaptic geometry and circuit integration</cite>.

# Practical synthesis: what “learning” looks like at the biological neuron

- Encoding: precise spike timing and correlated activity reshape synapses via STDP and related Hebbian rules, tagging events for plasticity through neuromodulatory co-activity and energy-permitting windows. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">Spike timing and neuromodulation co-determine LTP/LTD, with acetylcholine and related transmitters modulating NMDA receptors and STDP</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">Neuromodulatory control can provide global supervision for otherwise unsupervised STDP</cite>.
- Consolidation: activity-dependent transcription (CREB/IEGs), excitability shifts, and spine clustering select neurons into engram ensembles and potentiate synapses selectively as spontaneous and retrieval activity reinforce memory traces. <cite id="495966f1-0">CREB drives IEG expression that facilitates LTP and engram-specific synaptic increases across hippocampus, amygdala, and PFC</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-2">CREB levels mark neurons favored to participate in memory, integrating activation with molecular selection</cite>.
- Stability: homeostatic scaling and weight-dependent plasticity keep neurons biologically viable and receptive fields selective, preventing runaway potentiation or depression and aligning learning with energetic constraints. <cite id="0634f1b9-1">Homeostatic plasticity counters intrinsic instability of Hebbian rules and stabilizes firing</cite>. <cite id="0f6daaad-1">Soft-bound plasticity stabilizes weight distributions and yields selective receptive fields without extra normalization</cite>.
- Computation: synaptic and dendritic plasticity implement PCA/CCA-like objectives under sliding-threshold constraints, enabling neurons to learn principal features, correlations, and competitive selectivity within energy- and stability-limited budgets. <cite id="0f6daaad-0">BCM-like rules and dendritic compartments yield PCA-like and CCA-like learning with homeostatic constraints</cite>.

In sum, modern theory treats biological neurons as Bayesian-like adaptive machines: spike timing and co-activity supply priors and likelihoods for synaptic change; neuromodulators act as supervisory priors that license long-term modifications; homeostatic and energy constraints regularize learning; and molecular, dendritic, and synaptic remodeling implement engram selection and consolidation. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">Neuromodulatory control links unsupervised spike-timing events to supervised durability</cite>, <cite id="0634f1b9-1">homeostasis keeps learning biophysically feasible</cite>, and <cite id="0f6daaad-0,0f6daaad-1">computational frameworks like BCM unify Hebbian, spike-based, and dendritic mechanisms into selective, energy-aware learning rules</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-0">At the ensemble level, CREB/IEG-dependent consolidation and spine dynamics select circuits that represent and retrieve experience</cite>.

Modern theories of how biological neurons learn converge on a multi-timescale view in which precise spike timing and correlated activity shape synapses via local biochemical rules, neuromodulators provide supervisory “tags” that license long-term modifications, and homeostatic mechanisms keep networks biologically viable while learning proceeds. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">At the core are spike-timing–dependent plasticity (STDP) and related Hebbian rules that capture associative learning from temporally structured inputs</cite>, <cite id="0634f1b9-1">but purely Hebbian algorithms are intrinsically unstable without stabilizing negative feedback</cite>, so <cite id="0634f1b9-1">homeostatic plasticity evolved to regulate firing rates and synaptic strength</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">Neuromodulators (acetylcholine, monoamines, histamine, neuropeptides, hormones) tune plasticity, potentially providing global supervision for otherwise unsupervised rules like STDP</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-0">At longer timescales, activity-dependent transcription (CREB/IEGs), excitability changes, and spine clustering select and consolidate synaptic engrams in neuronal ensembles</cite>. <cite id="0f6daaad-0">Computationally, BCM-style rules and dendritic processing implement objectives akin to PCA/CCA with homeostatic constraints, tying synaptic modifications to variance and correlation maximization</cite>.

# Synaptic plasticity rules and temporal coding

Modern synaptic learning is driven by spike timing and correlated firing rather than only firing rates. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">STDP strengthens synapses when presynaptic spikes precede postsynaptic spikes and weakens them otherwise, enabling sequence learning and precise temporal coding</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-2">Experiments and theory link STDP to cortical map development, receptive-field sharpening, working memory, and associative learning, while emphasizing that it rarely acts alone</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-1">Some STDP variants can stabilize postsynaptic firing below critical frequencies, but in densely connected networks rapid runaway growth can require complementary homeostatic mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-1">In this sense, STDP provides a local, unsupervised learning signal, whereas neuromodulators provide regulatory or supervisory signals that determine whether changes are stored long term</cite>.

# Neuromodulatory tagging and long-term engram formation

A central advance is the integration of synaptic plasticity with neuromodulatory “tagging” that licenses durable modifications. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">Acetylcholine modulates NMDA receptor function and thereby plasticity, and neuromodulation of STDP extends beyond classical transmitters to neuropeptides, hormones, and immunological agents</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">Neuromodulatory control can provide global supervision to unsupervised rules, helping determine which plasticity events are committed to long-term memory</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-0">During encoding, synchronized sparse activity recruits neurons into engram cell ensembles; these neurons show prior connectivity and excitability that facilitate recruitment</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-0">Spine proximity and clustering, dendritic calcium/depolarization spikes, and enhanced CREB signaling prime neurons for recruitment, linking structural plasticity and transcriptional programs to engram selection</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-0">CREB-driven immediate early genes (IEGs) facilitate LTP and engram-specific increases in excitatory transmission in hippocampus, amygdala, and prefrontal cortex during consolidation</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-2">Converging evidence shows neurons activated and neurons expressing IEGs during learning/retrieval exhibit higher firing probability and altered synaptic plasticity, and that CREB levels mark neurons favored to enter a memory trace, effectively implementing a molecular selection mechanism</cite>.

# Stability and homeostasis: keeping learning within biological bounds

Instability is a key concern: purely Hebbian feedback can drive synapses to diverge or collapse and neurons to become either insensitive or hyperexcitable. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">Hebbian algorithms are intrinsically unstable because correlated firing leads to strengthening, which further increases correlated firing</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-1">Homeostatic plasticity discovered in the mid-1990s provides negative feedback that keeps postsynaptic activity near viable ranges, preventing neurons from becoming non-firable or overly sensitive</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-1">Even with STDP’s partial stabilization, explicit homeostatic mechanisms are often needed to counter rapid rate increases in highly connected networks</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-1">Quantitatively and mechanistically, links between STDP, BCM rules, and homeostatic scaling have been developed, including energy-energetic constraints that tie firing, membrane potential, and plasticity</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-2">Complementary forms of homeostatic plasticity—scaling total synaptic strength, activity-dependent intrinsic excitability, or history-dependent synaptic availability—coordinate with STDP to maintain circuit stability during development and learning</cite>.

# Computational perspective: objectives, competition, and coding

Modern theory also connects plasticity to explicit computational objectives. <cite id="0f6daaad-0">BCM theory provides a sliding-threshold rule that implements Hebbian plasticity constrained by postsynaptic activity, with dendritic compartments adding correlations across inputs; in two-compartment neurons, the learning rule corresponds to maximizing second-order moments and correlations while implementing PCA-like and CCA-like learning under homeostatic constraints</cite>. <cite id="0f6daaad-0">Somatic-only neurons perform PCA-like learning; dual-compartment neurons perform dual learning across compartments, with the objective weighted by a homeostatic parameter</cite>. <cite id="0f6daaad-1">BCM remains a leading unsupervised cortical plasticity model, with links to calcium dynamics and to STDP for spike-based learning; soft-bound (weight-dependent) plasticity—less LTP for strong synapses and roughly linear LTD percentage for weak synapses—naturally reproduces observed weight distributions and avoids unbounded growth</cite>. <cite id="0f6daaad-2">In network models, BCM-like excitatory plasticity with sliding thresholds and pruning implements competitive learning and stimulus selectivity, while homeostatic inhibitory plasticity stabilizes target firing rates, capturing balanced competition between excitatory and inhibitory inputs</cite>.

# Dendritic nonlinearities and spine structural plasticity

Learning is not confined to the soma: dendrites integrate inputs nonlinearly and remodel synapses to implement cell- and compartment-specific transformations. <cite id="0f6daaad-0">Dendritic activity supports LTP generated by coincident proximal and distal inputs, and BCM-like rules generalize to dendritic compartments, yielding dual PCA/CCA learning when somatic and dendritic inputs are integrated</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-0">Spine clustering near preexisting spines induces local dendritic calcium and depolarization, enhancing excitability to promote recruitment into engrams, while CREB signaling and IEGs support consolidation and engram-specific synaptic potentiation</cite>. Together these mechanisms allow neurons to compute correlations and mixtures of features at different spatial scales while maintaining energy-constrained dynamics and selective receptive fields.

# From single-cell rules to circuits and systems

Modern theories explain learning as emergent from interacting synaptic, cellular, and circuit mechanisms. <cite id="0634f1b9-2">Unless synaptic changes are coordinated across synapses and neuronal properties, stability and functionality degrade; thus homeostatic and developmental constraints partner with STDP to shape maps, receptive fields, working memory, and associative learning</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-0">Synchronized sparse recruitment, CREB/IEG-dependent consolidation, and spine remodeling select engram cell ensembles that encode specific experiences</cite>. <cite id="0f6daaad-0">At the computational system level, BCM-like and dendritic learning rules implement dimensionality reduction and correlation alignment objectives, enabling neurons to extract principal components, canonical correlations, and selective receptive fields under homeostatic constraints</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-1">Neuromodulatory control bridges local spike timing events to global supervision over days to weeks, aligning synaptic tagging with energy and neuroenergetic limits, and providing a framework to reconcile short-term plasticity with long-term memory storage</cite>.

# Open frontiers and integrative principles

Two intertwined challenges define “modern” progress. First, supervisory mechanisms: <cite id="0634f1b9-0">neuromodulatory control of STDP, spanning classic transmitters and peptides, likely gates whether transient spike-timing events become durable engrams, but the precise rules and timescales across systems remain under active study</cite>. Second, stability-energy coupling: <cite id="0634f1b9-1">homeostatic plasticity, energy supply, and firing rates are deeply intertwined, suggesting a thermodynamic view in which synaptic modification must respect mitochondrial constraints and network energetics</cite>. On the computational side, <cite id="0f6daaad-1">weight-dependent plasticity and soft bounds can stabilize distributions without explicit global normalization, linking microscopic calcium- and spike-based rules to macroscopic selectivity and robustness</cite>. Finally, engram selection integrates molecular and structural plasticity: <cite id="495966f1-0">CREB/IEG signaling modulates excitability and promotes spine clustering that increases local dendritic calcium, coupling transcriptional programs to synaptic geometry and circuit integration</cite>.

# Practical synthesis: what “learning” looks like at the biological neuron

- Encoding: precise spike timing and correlated activity reshape synapses via STDP and related Hebbian rules, tagging events for plasticity through neuromodulatory co-activity and energy-permitting windows. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">Spike timing and neuromodulation co-determine LTP/LTD, with acetylcholine and related transmitters modulating NMDA receptors and STDP</cite>. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">Neuromodulatory control can provide global supervision for otherwise unsupervised STDP</cite>.
- Consolidation: activity-dependent transcription (CREB/IEGs), excitability shifts, and spine clustering select neurons into engram ensembles and potentiate synapses selectively as spontaneous and retrieval activity reinforce memory traces. <cite id="495966f1-0">CREB drives IEG expression that facilitates LTP and engram-specific synaptic increases across hippocampus, amygdala, and PFC</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-2">CREB levels mark neurons favored to participate in memory, integrating activation with molecular selection</cite>.
- Stability: homeostatic scaling and weight-dependent plasticity keep neurons biologically viable and receptive fields selective, preventing runaway potentiation or depression and aligning learning with energetic constraints. <cite id="0634f1b9-1">Homeostatic plasticity counters intrinsic instability of Hebbian rules and stabilizes firing</cite>. <cite id="0f6daaad-1">Soft-bound plasticity stabilizes weight distributions and yields selective receptive fields without extra normalization</cite>.
- Computation: synaptic and dendritic plasticity implement PCA/CCA-like objectives under sliding-threshold constraints, enabling neurons to learn principal features, correlations, and competitive selectivity within energy- and stability-limited budgets. <cite id="0f6daaad-0">BCM-like rules and dendritic compartments yield PCA-like and CCA-like learning with homeostatic constraints</cite>.

In sum, modern theory treats biological neurons as Bayesian-like adaptive machines: spike timing and co-activity supply priors and likelihoods for synaptic change; neuromodulators act as supervisory priors that license long-term modifications; homeostatic and energy constraints regularize learning; and molecular, dendritic, and synaptic remodeling implement engram selection and consolidation. <cite id="0634f1b9-0">Neuromodulatory control links unsupervised spike-timing events to supervised durability</cite>, <cite id="0634f1b9-1">homeostasis keeps learning biophysically feasible</cite>, and <cite id="0f6daaad-0,0f6daaad-1">computational frameworks like BCM unify Hebbian, spike-based, and dendritic mechanisms into selective, energy-aware learning rules</cite>. <cite id="495966f1-0">At the ensemble level, CREB/IEG-dependent consolidation and spine dynamics select circuits that represent and retrieve experience</cite>.

Title: Homeostatic Plasticity and STDP: Keeping a Neuron's Cool in a Fluctuating World
Snippet: Spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) offers a powerful means of forming and modifying neural circuits. Experimental and theoretical studies have demonstrated its potential usefulness for functions as varied as cortical map development, sharpening of sensory receptive fields, working memory, and associative learning. Even so, it is unlikely that STDP works alone. Unless changes in synaptic strength are coordinated across multiple synapses and with other neuronal properties, it is difficult to maintain the stability and functionality of neural circuits. Moreover, there are certain features of early postnatal development (e.g., rapid changes in sensory input) that threaten neural circuit stability in ways that STDP may not be well placed to counter. These considerations have led researchers to investigate additional types of plasticity, complementary to STDP, that may serve to constrain synaptic weights and/or neuronal firing. These are collectively known as “homeostatic plasticity” and include schemes that control the total synaptic strength of a neuron, that modulate its intrinsic excitability as a function of average activity, or that make the ability of synapses to undergo Hebbian modification depend upon their history of use. In this article, we will review the experimental evidence for homeostatic forms of plasticity and consider how they might interact with STDP during development, and learning and memory.

Title: Shaping memories via stress: a synaptic engram perspective.
Snippet: It has been suggested that imbalanced excitatory-inhibitory synaptic inputs (101) and the degree of synaptic connectivity (33) of engram cell ensembles modulate memory processing, highlighting the pivotal role of synaptic engrams in memory. 

During memory encoding, the synchronized activity of sparsely dispersed neurons promotes neuronal recruitment into an engram cell ensemble (102). These neurons already display relatively high and stable excitatory synaptic connectivity with slow synaptic turnover prior to learning (103). The recruitment of neurons into an engram cell ensemble may be supported by their capacity to form spines that are in close proximity to preexisting spines and induce spine clustering (34). It has been suggested that spine clusters induce local dendritic calcium and depolarization spikes that enhance neuronal excitability (54). Moreover, synaptic activity may enhance CREB signaling (104), which enhances excitability to prime neurons for recruitment into an engram cell ensemble (105)(106)(107). Neuronal excitability influences synaptic transmission (99,100), and CREB may modulate retrograde synaptic mechanisms that promote neuronal recruitment into an engram cell ensemble (33). Thus, while natural fluctuations in excitability as well as prior neuronal activity likely contribute to memory allocation (108), (prior) synaptic connectivity, activity, and plasticity can affect excitability to promote the recruitment of neurons for memory allocation. 

Synaptic mechanisms also support memory consolidation through engram cells. CREB drives the expression of immediate early genes (IEGs) (109,110), which are primary responsive factors to neuronal activity that are commonly used to study engram cells. Acting largely as transcription factors, IEGs can facilitate LTP (111), which possibly contributes to the engram cell-specific, learning-induced increase in spontaneous excitatory synaptic transmission in the hippocampus (23,28,31) and evoked excitatory synaptic transmission in the amygdala (112) and PFC (113).

Title: Which Neurons Will Be the Engram - Activated Neurons and/or More Excitable Neurons?
Snippet: Therefore, many researchers have focused on the neuronal population, which is activated by learning, to search for the engram. Recently, the firing pattern comparison between the populations of neurons marked by neuronal activation during learning and the populations of neurons that express immediate early genes (IEG) during retrieval revealed that neurons, which were activated by learning, showed relatively higher firing probability at memory retrieval [8,9]. In addition to these results, it was shown that neurons whose synaptic plasticity was changed by learning have higher firing rate during retrieval as seen in electrophysiological experiments [10]. These results have shown a possibility that neuronal ensembles, which were activated by learning, could be preferentially recruited into the memory-encoding population and eventually become the memory engram. 

Meanwhile, more and more compelling evidence suggest that transcription factor cAMP responsive element binding protein (CREB) plays a significant role in governing which LA neurons will participate in a given memory trace [11]. CREB research first started from revealing that CREB overexpression in small portion (~20%) of amygdala neurons could enhance fear memory [12]. The same group of researchers further developed the study by showing LA neurons with increased CREB levels are favorably recruited to involve in the memory trace. Sheena Josselyn and her colleagues brilliantly hypothesized that neurons overexpressing CREB at the time of learning shall win the "competition" to become part of the memory trace [13], and proved this right through biological imaging technique. In other words, neuronal population which contains relatively high level of CREB at the time of the learning also has been proposed as a candidate of the engram [12,13]. Indeed there are many other protein molecules that may be crucial for the memory allocation process. So far CREB is the most well studied and understood factor in governing the selection of neurons into the memory trace, but considering the complex and dynamic nature of memory formation and storage, it is unquestionable that there are many other unknown protein candidates to be resolved by future studies.

Therefore, many researchers have focused on the neuronal population, which is activated by learning, to search for the engram. Recently, the firing pattern comparison between the populations of neurons marked by neuronal activation during learning and the populations of neurons that express immediate early genes (IEG) during retrieval revealed that neurons, which were activated by learning, showed relatively higher firing probability at memory retrieval [8,9]. In addition to these results, it was shown that neurons whose synaptic plasticity was changed by learning have higher firing rate during retrieval as seen in electrophysiological experiments [10]. These results have shown a possibility that neuronal ensembles, which were activated by learning, could be preferentially recruited into the memory-encoding population and eventually become the memory engram. 

Meanwhile, more and more compelling evidence suggest that transcription factor cAMP responsive element binding protein (CREB) plays a significant role in governing which LA neurons will participate in a given memory trace [11]. CREB research first started from revealing that CREB overexpression in small portion (~20%) of amygdala neurons could enhance fear memory [12]. The same group of researchers further developed the study by showing LA neurons with increased CREB levels are favorably recruited to involve in the memory trace. Sheena Josselyn and her colleagues brilliantly hypothesized that neurons overexpressing CREB at the time of learning shall win the "competition" to become part of the memory trace [13], and proved this right through biological imaging technique. In other words, neuronal population which contains relatively high level of CREB at the time of the learning also has been proposed as a candidate of the engram [12,13]. Indeed there are many other protein molecules that may be crucial for the memory allocation process. So far CREB is the most well studied and understood factor in governing the selection of neurons into the memory trace, but considering the complex and dynamic nature of memory formation and storage, it is unquestionable that there are many other unknown protein candidates to be resolved by future studies.

It has been suggested that imbalanced excitatory-inhibitory synaptic inputs (101) and the degree of synaptic connectivity (33) of engram cell ensembles modulate memory processing, highlighting the pivotal role of synaptic engrams in memory. 

During memory encoding, the synchronized activity of sparsely dispersed neurons promotes neuronal recruitment into an engram cell ensemble (102). These neurons already display relatively high and stable excitatory synaptic connectivity with slow synaptic turnover prior to learning (103). The recruitment of neurons into an engram cell ensemble may be supported by their capacity to form spines that are in close proximity to preexisting spines and induce spine clustering (34). It has been suggested that spine clusters induce local dendritic calcium and depolarization spikes that enhance neuronal excitability (54). Moreover, synaptic activity may enhance CREB signaling (104), which enhances excitability to prime neurons for recruitment into an engram cell ensemble (105)(106)(107). Neuronal excitability influences synaptic transmission (99,100), and CREB may modulate retrograde synaptic mechanisms that promote neuronal recruitment into an engram cell ensemble (33). Thus, while natural fluctuations in excitability as well as prior neuronal activity likely contribute to memory allocation (108), (prior) synaptic connectivity, activity, and plasticity can affect excitability to promote the recruitment of neurons for memory allocation. 

Synaptic mechanisms also support memory consolidation through engram cells. CREB drives the expression of immediate early genes (IEGs) (109,110), which are primary responsive factors to neuronal activity that are commonly used to study engram cells. Acting largely as transcription factors, IEGs can facilitate LTP (111), which possibly contributes to the engram cell-specific, learning-induced increase in spontaneous excitatory synaptic transmission in the hippocampus (23,28,31) and evoked excitatory synaptic transmission in the amygdala (112) and PFC (113).

Below we synthesize learning mechanisms that show broad, cross-system operation in biological neurons. “Universal” here means mechanisms that emerge across brain regions, neuron classes, and preparations, while acknowledging cell-type-, system-, and timescale-specific modulations documented in experiments and theory.

Scope and definition
- Learning in biological neurons is expressed through activity-dependent modifications of synaptic efficacy, intrinsic excitability, and circuit-wide balance, implemented over multiple timescales from milliseconds to years. <cite id="9e942828-0">Metaplasticity has been shown to take place through various molecular pathways and to be critical for the stabilization of learned statistics</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-1">Experiments show that STDP is one aspect of long-term change, with direction and extent of modification depending on presynaptic/post-synaptic activity patterns, synaptic location, neuromodulators, timescales (including homeostatic processes), and history (metaplasticity)</cite>.

Core synaptic plasticity rules: Hebbian/associative and spike-timing–dependent
- Associative (Hebbian) plasticity links correlated pre- and postsynaptic activity and underlies experience-driven refinement from development to learning. <cite id="9e942828-3">Homosynaptic plasticity requires presynaptic activation and is input-specific and associative; associative plasticity ranges from developmental wiring to causal relation extraction</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-1">Associative plasticity depends on correlated activity of pre- and postsynaptic neurons and is a core phenomenology across systems</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-3">STDP is a biologically plausible model of in vivo synaptic modification across brain regions such as corticostriatum, barrel cortex, and visual cortex, with presynaptic-before-postsynaptic spikes typically inducing LTP and vice versa for LTD via a narrow, system-specific millisecond window</cite>.
- Spike-timing–dependent plasticity (STDP) operates as a temporally asymmetric Hebbian rule and is widely reported across circuits and synapse types. <cite id="d2c67462-0">STDP adjusts synaptic strength via a spike timing difference–dependent update rule and has been linked to temporal sequence learning, coincidence detection, navigation, and competitive development</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-3">STDP has been reported in excitatory and inhibitory synapses and can be modified by cholinergic, dopaminergic, and adrenergic signaling</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-4">Single-pair STDP with a single postsynaptic spike occurs in hippocampus, optic tectum, and neocortex, though pairing outcomes can vary by local inhibition and baseline conditions</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-2">Human hippocampal synapses can exhibit a wide temporal window for STDP, contrasting with some rodent preparations, underscoring species- and system-specific windows within a universal causal ordering principle</cite>.
- Spike-rate–dependent plasticity and frequency coding shape learning beyond precise timing: higher-frequency stimulation increases timing-dependent LTP, and rate/sequence features drive long-term changes. <cite id="d2c67462-3">Spontaneous spiking and higher spike frequencies modulate STDP strength, with higher frequencies increasing timing-dependent LTP</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-1">Direction and extent of synaptic change depend not only on spike timing but on spike rates and local conditions, with homeostatic processes acting on slower timescales</cite>.
- Mechanistic grounding: calcium dynamics and presynaptic release probability provide common currency. <cite id="9e942828-0">Activity-dependent induction thresholds and BCM-like metaplasticity can stabilize learning and have biophysical implementations</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-1">A calcium-based phenomenological model reproduces rich STDP phenomenology across experiments</cite>.

Homeostatic stabilization: synaptic scaling, E/I balance, and heterosynaptic mechanisms
- Synaptic scaling adjusts overall efficacy to maintain stable activity and signal-to-noise, preventing runaway potentiation or depression. <cite id="9e942828-2">Synaptic saturation in linear STDP can be addressed by slightly stronger LTD than LTP and by stabilization mechanisms such as synaptic scaling that reduce total synaptic strength changes per neuron, preventing runaway plasticity</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-3">Homeostasis of synaptic weights at the single-cell level and excitation/inhibition balance at network level maintain operating ranges; homosynaptic and heterosynaptic forms of plasticity can either disrupt or restore balance</cite>.
- Heterosynaptic plasticity redistributes synaptic strengths to preserve total activity or firing rates, providing a route to stable learning under changing inputs. <cite id="9e942828-3">Heterosynaptic plasticity contributes to homeostatic roles; homosynaptic plasticity is input-specific and associative while heterosynaptic adjusts many synapses simultaneously to counteract imbalance</cite>.
- Degeneracy across mechanisms: encoding plasticity coexists with activity homeostasis and stability across synaptic, intrinsic, glial, and structural components. <cite id="9e942828-4">Encoding-driven plasticity, activity homeostasis, and stable learning emerge via disparate combinations of synaptic, intrinsic, glial, and structural plasticity, with experimental evidence for activity- or experience-dependent plasticity in each component</cite>.

Intrinsic neuronal learning: spike-frequency adaptation and dynamical imprinting
- Spike-frequency adaptation (SFA) shapes synaptic learning by rescaling dynamic range and providing a learned nonlinear transfer function tuned to input statistics. <cite id="1f36c3b4-0">SFA enhances information transmission in sensory spiking neurons by rescaling dynamic range to match stimulus statistics</cite>. <cite id="1f36c3b4-1">Triplet-based STDP that interacts with SFA can yield near-optimal information transmission and matches in vitro theta-linked dynamics, explaining target-cell specificity and differences between principal-cell and fast-spiking interneuron STDP</cite>.

- Spike timing windows vary across systems and species, implying diversity within universality. <cite id="d2c67462-2">Human hippocampal synapses exhibit a wide temporal window for STDP, contrasting with rodent hippocampus</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-3">Across regions, the causal order of spikes suffices for LTP/LTD, but precise windows and modulatory influences differ</cite>.

Putting it together: what is universal and what is variable
- Mechanisms that recur across biological neurons include: activity-correlation–dependent homosynaptic potentiation/depression (Hebbian/associative) and spike-timing–dependent synaptic modification; rate- and timing-based forms of plasticity shaped by spike history and frequency; heterosynaptic and spike-frequency adaptation that stabilize total activity and rescale dynamic range; and history- and timescale-dependent metaplasticity (BCM/running-man) that prevents saturation and stabilizes learned selectivity. <cite id="9e942828-3">Homosynaptic associative plasticity and heterosynaptic mechanisms provide complementary routes to encoding and stabilization</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-3">STDP and frequency/sequence coding are broadly observed across brain regions and synapse types, with neuromodulatory control</cite>. <cite id="1f36c3b4-0">SFA improves information transmission by adapting to stimulus statistics</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-0">Metaplasticity and BCM-like rules stabilize learning</cite>.
- These mechanisms interact with intrinsic excitability, dendritic nonlinearities, and oscillatory dynamics, yielding system-specific manifestations while preserving universal computational roles: encoding selectivity via spike timing, maintaining activity homeostasis via scaling/heterosynaptic rules, and shaping transfer functions via adaptation. <cite id="1f36c3b4-1">Triplet-STDP interacting with adaptation achieves near-optimal transmission and explains target-cell specificity across principal cells and interneurons</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-4">Oscillatory phase dependence in hippocampal and olfactory circuits constrains how plasticity supports memory imprinting and retrieval</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-4">Concurrent encoding, stability, and homeostasis emerge from combinations of synaptic, intrinsic, glial, and structural plasticity</cite>.

Practical implications and caveats
- Claims of “universality” must be qualified by location, receptor/gene expression, neuromodulatory state, dendritic compartment, and timescales. <cite id="9e942828-1">The direction and extent of synaptic modification depend on activity patterns, location, neuromodulators, and history; homeostatic processes act on slower time scales</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-3">Spike timing windows and frequency dependence are synapse- and system-specific</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-4">Local inhibition can invert or prevent plasticity outcomes under identical pairing protocols</cite>.
- Nonetheless, converging evidence across preparations supports a minimal set of cross-neuronal learning mechanisms: Hebbian/associative and STDP for causal relation and temporal sequence learning; rate- and frequency-based potentiation/depression; heterosynaptic scaling for E/I and total activity balance; spike-frequency adaptation for dynamic-range compression and nonlinear transfer; and metaplasticity to stabilize and regulate learning over multiple timescales. <cite id="9e942828-3">Homosynaptic and heterosynaptic plasticity jointly realize encoding and homeostasis</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-3">STDP and frequency/sequence dependence are broadly reported across excitatory and inhibitory synapses</cite>. <cite id="1f36c3b4-1">Adaptation-aware STDP achieves near-optimal transmission and matches in vivo theta dynamics</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-0">Metaplasticity provides a universal stabilizer of learned statistics through history-dependent induction thresholds</cite>.

Summary
- Universally operating learning mechanisms in biological neurons encompass: activity-correlation–based homosynaptic plasticity and spike-timing–dependent plasticity; spike-rate–dependent forms that integrate frequency and history; homeostatic synaptic scaling and heterosynaptic mechanisms that maintain excitation/inhibition and firing-rate balance; spike-frequency adaptation that tunes transfer functions to input statistics; and metaplasticity that conditions plasticity on past history and timescales. <cite id="9e942828-0">Metaplasticity stabilizes learned statistics and can be implemented via activity-dependent thresholds</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-1">These mechanisms are shaped by location, neuromodulators, and timescales, with homeostatic processes on slower timescales</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-2">Even the temporal window for STDP can be broad in adult human synapses</cite>. <cite id="1f36c3b4-0">Adaptation and STDP cooperate to optimize information transmission in sensory neurons</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-4">Inhibitory microcircuits and oscillatory context provide universal scaffolds that shape plasticity expression across brain areas</cite>. Together, these mechanisms provide a coherent, cross-neuronal basis for learning while remaining flexible and system-specific in their details.

This process precisely adjusts the strength of connections between neurons based on the relative timing of their electrical impulses, known as action potentials or spikes [1,2]. This intricate timing-dependent modulation is widely regarded as a cornerstone for how the brain acquires and retains information, as well as how its complex neuronal circuits undergo development and refinement throughout an organism's lifespan [3].

where A + , A − > 0 are the maximal potentiation and depression amplitudes, and τ + , τ − are decay time constants. Small positive ∆t (presynaptic before postsynaptic) is interpreted as causal, producing strong potentiation; small negative ∆t (postsynaptic before presynaptic) is interpreted as anti-causal, producing strong depression. This yields an asymmetric, causality-driven plasticity window. 

The core principle of STDP dictates that if a presynaptic neuron fires its spike a few milliseconds before a postsynaptic neuron generates its own action potential, the synaptic connection between them typically undergoes Long-Term Potentiation (LTP), signifying a strengthening of that connection. Conversely, if the presynaptic spike arrives after the postsynaptic spike, the same synapse experiences Long-Term Depression (LTD), leading to its weakening [1]. This specific temporal window, often termed the STDP function or learning window, is not universal but can exhibit variations across different types of synapses, reflecting the diverse computational roles of various brain regions. 

The precise detection of these millisecond-scale spike timings is often mediated by NMDA receptors, which function as critical coincidence detectors within the synaptic machinery [4].

It is determined by the temporal order of action potential initiations and the narrow time between subsequent action potentials. In general, activation of the presynaptic cell immediately before activation of the postsynaptic cell leads to timing-dependent LTP, while activating the presynaptic neuron immediately after the postsynaptic cell elicits timing-dependent LTD [68,69]. The time window between these activations needs to be in the order of milliseconds, is specific for each synapse and depends on receptor kinetics, current densities and the release of retrograde messengers such as endocannabinoids [69]. Title: STDP in Adaptive Neurons Gives Close-To-Optimal Information Transmission
Snippet: Spike-frequency adaptation is known to enhance the transmission of information in sensory spiking neurons by rescaling the dynamic range for input processing, matching it to the temporal statistics of the sensory stimulus. Achieving maximal information transmission has also been recently postulated as a role for spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). However, the link between optimal plasticity and STDP in cortex remains loose, as does the relationship between STDP and adaptation processes. We investigate how STDP, as described by recent minimal models derived from experimental data, influences the quality of information transmission in an adapting neuron. We show that a phenomenological model based on triplets of spikes yields almost the same information rate as an optimal model specially designed to this end. In contrast, the standard pair-based model of STDP does not improve information transmission as much. This result holds not only for additive STDP with hard weight bounds, known to produce bimodal distributions of synaptic weights, but also for weight-dependent STDP in the context of unimodal but skewed weight distributions. We analyze the similarities between the triplet model and the optimal learning rule, and find that the triplet effect is an important feature of the optimal model when the neuron is adaptive. If STDP is optimized for information transmission, it must take into account the dynamical properties of the postsynaptic cell, which might explain the target-cell specificity of STDP. In particular, it accounts for the differences found in vitro between STDP at excitatory synapses onto principal cells and those onto fast-spiking interneurons.

Title: The Origin of Adaptation in the Auditory Pathway of Locusts Is Specific to Cell Type and Function
Snippet: We investigated the origin of spike frequency adaptation within a layered sensory network: the auditory pathway of locusts. Spike frequency adaptation as observed in an individual neuron may arise because of intrinsic or presynaptic adaptation mechanisms. Title: Hebbian Imprinting and Retrieval in Oscillatory Neural Networks
Snippet: We introduce a model of generalized Hebbian learning and retrieval in oscillatory neural networks modeling cortical areas such as hippocampus and olfactory cortex. Recent experiments have shown that synaptic plasticity depends on spike timing, especially on synapses from excitatory pyramidal cells, in hippocampus, and in sensory and cerebellar cortex. Here we study how such plasticity can be used to form memories and input representations when the neural dynamics are oscillatory, as is common in the brain (particularly in the hippocampus and olfactory cortex). Learning is assumed to occur in a phase of neural plasticity, in which the network is clamped to external teaching signals. By suitable manipulation of the nonlinearity of the neurons or the oscillation frequencies during learning, the model can be made, in a retrieval phase, either to categorize new inputs or to map them, in a continuous fashion, onto the space spanned by the imprinted patterns. We identify the first of these possibilities with the function of olfactory cortex and the second with the observed response characteristics of place cells in hippocampus. We investigate both kinds of networks analytically and by computer simulations, and we link the models with experimental findings, exploring, in particular, how the spike timing dependence of the synaptic plasticity constrains the computational function of the network and vice versa.

Below we synthesize learning mechanisms that show broad, cross-system operation in biological neurons. “Universal” here means mechanisms that emerge across brain regions, neuron classes, and preparations, while acknowledging cell-type-, system-, and timescale-specific modulations documented in experiments and theory.

Scope and definition
- Learning in biological neurons is expressed through activity-dependent modifications of synaptic efficacy, intrinsic excitability, and circuit-wide balance, implemented over multiple timescales from milliseconds to years. <cite id="9e942828-0">Metaplasticity has been shown to take place through various molecular pathways and to be critical for the stabilization of learned statistics</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-1">Experiments show that STDP is one aspect of long-term change, with direction and extent of modification depending on presynaptic/post-synaptic activity patterns, synaptic location, neuromodulators, timescales (including homeostatic processes), and history (metaplasticity)</cite>.

Core synaptic plasticity rules: Hebbian/associative and spike-timing–dependent
- Associative (Hebbian) plasticity links correlated pre- and postsynaptic activity and underlies experience-driven refinement from development to learning. <cite id="9e942828-3">Homosynaptic plasticity requires presynaptic activation and is input-specific and associative; associative plasticity ranges from developmental wiring to causal relation extraction</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-1">Associative plasticity depends on correlated activity of pre- and postsynaptic neurons and is a core phenomenology across systems</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-3">STDP is a biologically plausible model of in vivo synaptic modification across brain regions such as corticostriatum, barrel cortex, and visual cortex, with presynaptic-before-postsynaptic spikes typically inducing LTP and vice versa for LTD via a narrow, system-specific millisecond window</cite>.
- Spike-timing–dependent plasticity (STDP) operates as a temporally asymmetric Hebbian rule and is widely reported across circuits and synapse types. <cite id="d2c67462-0">STDP adjusts synaptic strength via a spike timing difference–dependent update rule and has been linked to temporal sequence learning, coincidence detection, navigation, and competitive development</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-3">STDP has been reported in excitatory and inhibitory synapses and can be modified by cholinergic, dopaminergic, and adrenergic signaling</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-4">Single-pair STDP with a single postsynaptic spike occurs in hippocampus, optic tectum, and neocortex, though pairing outcomes can vary by local inhibition and baseline conditions</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-2">Human hippocampal synapses can exhibit a wide temporal window for STDP, contrasting with some rodent preparations, underscoring species- and system-specific windows within a universal causal ordering principle</cite>.
- Spike-rate–dependent plasticity and frequency coding shape learning beyond precise timing: higher-frequency stimulation increases timing-dependent LTP, and rate/sequence features drive long-term changes. <cite id="d2c67462-3">Spontaneous spiking and higher spike frequencies modulate STDP strength, with higher frequencies increasing timing-dependent LTP</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-1">Direction and extent of synaptic change depend not only on spike timing but on spike rates and local conditions, with homeostatic processes acting on slower timescales</cite>.
- Mechanistic grounding: calcium dynamics and presynaptic release probability provide common currency. <cite id="9e942828-0">Activity-dependent induction thresholds and BCM-like metaplasticity can stabilize learning and have biophysical implementations</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-1">A calcium-based phenomenological model reproduces rich STDP phenomenology across experiments</cite>.

Homeostatic stabilization: synaptic scaling, E/I balance, and heterosynaptic mechanisms
- Synaptic scaling adjusts overall efficacy to maintain stable activity and signal-to-noise, preventing runaway potentiation or depression. <cite id="9e942828-2">Synaptic saturation in linear STDP can be addressed by slightly stronger LTD than LTP and by stabilization mechanisms such as synaptic scaling that reduce total synaptic strength changes per neuron, preventing runaway plasticity</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-3">Homeostasis of synaptic weights at the single-cell level and excitation/inhibition balance at network level maintain operating ranges; homosynaptic and heterosynaptic forms of plasticity can either disrupt or restore balance</cite>.
- Heterosynaptic plasticity redistributes synaptic strengths to preserve total activity or firing rates, providing a route to stable learning under changing inputs. <cite id="9e942828-3">Heterosynaptic plasticity contributes to homeostatic roles; homosynaptic plasticity is input-specific and associative while heterosynaptic adjusts many synapses simultaneously to counteract imbalance</cite>.
- Degeneracy across mechanisms: encoding plasticity coexists with activity homeostasis and stability across synaptic, intrinsic, glial, and structural components. <cite id="9e942828-4">Encoding-driven plasticity, activity homeostasis, and stable learning emerge via disparate combinations of synaptic, intrinsic, glial, and structural plasticity, with experimental evidence for activity- or experience-dependent plasticity in each component</cite>.

Intrinsic neuronal learning: spike-frequency adaptation and dynamical imprinting
- Spike-frequency adaptation (SFA) shapes synaptic learning by rescaling dynamic range and providing a learned nonlinear transfer function tuned to input statistics. <cite id="1f36c3b4-0">SFA enhances information transmission in sensory spiking neurons by rescaling dynamic range to match stimulus statistics</cite>. <cite id="1f36c3b4-1">Triplet-based STDP that interacts with SFA can yield near-optimal information transmission and matches in vitro theta-linked dynamics, explaining target-cell specificity and differences between principal-cell and fast-spiking interneuron STDP</cite>.
- Adaptation can arise from intrinsic currents and presynaptic mechanisms and is tailored to cell function across sensory pathways and systems. <cite id="1f36c3b4-2">Across locust auditory pathway interneurons, adaptation origins differ: some show balanced intrinsic and presynaptic contributions, others predominantly inherit adaptation from inhibitory inputs, and others rely primarily on intrinsic spike-triggered adaptation, with distinct time courses linked to processing roles</cite>.
- Dendritic and somatic adaptation, plateau potentials, and oscillatory context add universal features of intrinsic plasticity. <cite id="1f36c3b4-3">Two-compartment models with spike-triggered adaptation at the soma and activity-dependent dendritic transfer functions enable adaptive spiking, with backpropagating action potentials and dendritic adaptation shaping computation</cite>. <cite id="1f36c3b4-1">Optimal learning rules explicitly depend on the neuron’s transfer function and show that triplet effects with timescales near adaptation (≈100–150 ms) are crucial for performance</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-4">Oscillatory context in hippocampus and olfactory cortex constrains how spike timing dependence of plasticity supports memory formation and retrieval</cite>.

Universal organizers of plasticity: metaplasticity and running-man/BCM
- Metaplasticity adjusts the plasticity rule based on prior synaptic history and timescales, preventing saturation and enabling selective memory stabilization. <cite id="9e942828-0">Metaplasticity promotes conditional, history-dependent persistent changes in synaptic weights; BCM theory provides a precursor with activity-dependent induction thresholds and has been linked to STDP and hippocampal priming experiments</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-2">Stabilization mechanisms like synaptic scaling and metaplasticity can naturally emerge from cellular mechanisms with stabilizing influence</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-1">Metaplasticity accounts for multi-scale plasticity and history dependence, with neuromodulation and location further shaping induction</cite>.
- Running-man/BCM dynamics and conditional thresholds implement universal stabilization of selectivity and rate homeostasis. <cite id="9e942828-0">An mSTDP model with fast and slow induction processes reproduces STDP, short-term competition, and long-term priming-like regulation, offering a path to prevent catastrophic forgetting</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-2">BCM-like activity-dependent thresholds prevent runaway potentiation and can arise from biophysical stabilization, tying metaplasticity and synaptic scaling to cellular mechanisms</cite>.

Constraints on universality: neuromodulation, location, spike timing windows, and competition
- Plasticity is not purely algorithmic: it depends on receptor kinetics, location on dendrites, neuromodulators, spike frequency, and inhibitory microcircuitry. <cite id="d2c67462-3">The STDP time window is specific to each synapse and depends on receptor kinetics, current densities, and retrograde messengers such as endocannabinoids; higher frequencies increase LTP</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-1">Direction and extent of modification depend on presynaptic/post-synaptic activity, synaptic location, neuromodulators, and history, with homeostatic plasticity on slower timescales</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-4">Pairing protocols can yield LTP, LTD, or no change independently of baseline strength and are modulated by GABA-A inhibition, indicating strong local circuit control</cite>.
- Spike timing windows vary across systems and species, implying diversity within universality. <cite id="d2c67462-2">Human hippocampal synapses exhibit a wide temporal window for STDP, contrasting with rodent hippocampus</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-3">Across regions, the causal order of spikes suffices for LTP/LTD, but precise windows and modulatory influences differ</cite>.

Putting it together: what is universal and what is variable
- Mechanisms that recur across biological neurons include: activity-correlation–dependent homosynaptic potentiation/depression (Hebbian/associative) and spike-timing–dependent synaptic modification; rate- and timing-based forms of plasticity shaped by spike history and frequency; heterosynaptic and spike-frequency adaptation that stabilize total activity and rescale dynamic range; and history- and timescale-dependent metaplasticity (BCM/running-man) that prevents saturation and stabilizes learned selectivity. <cite id="9e942828-3">Homosynaptic associative plasticity and heterosynaptic mechanisms provide complementary routes to encoding and stabilization</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-3">STDP and frequency/sequence coding are broadly observed across brain regions and synapse types, with neuromodulatory control</cite>. <cite id="1f36c3b4-0">SFA improves information transmission by adapting to stimulus statistics</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-0">Metaplasticity and BCM-like rules stabilize learning</cite>.
- These mechanisms interact with intrinsic excitability, dendritic nonlinearities, and oscillatory dynamics, yielding system-specific manifestations while preserving universal computational roles: encoding selectivity via spike timing, maintaining activity homeostasis via scaling/heterosynaptic rules, and shaping transfer functions via adaptation. <cite id="1f36c3b4-1">Triplet-STDP interacting with adaptation achieves near-optimal transmission and explains target-cell specificity across principal cells and interneurons</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-4">Oscillatory phase dependence in hippocampal and olfactory circuits constrains how plasticity supports memory imprinting and retrieval</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-4">Concurrent encoding, stability, and homeostasis emerge from combinations of synaptic, intrinsic, glial, and structural plasticity</cite>.

Practical implications and caveats
- Claims of “universality” must be qualified by location, receptor/gene expression, neuromodulatory state, dendritic compartment, and timescales. <cite id="9e942828-1">The direction and extent of synaptic modification depend on activity patterns, location, neuromodulators, and history; homeostatic processes act on slower time scales</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-3">Spike timing windows and frequency dependence are synapse- and system-specific</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-4">Local inhibition can invert or prevent plasticity outcomes under identical pairing protocols</cite>.
- Nonetheless, converging evidence across preparations supports a minimal set of cross-neuronal learning mechanisms: Hebbian/associative and STDP for causal relation and temporal sequence learning; rate- and frequency-based potentiation/depression; heterosynaptic scaling for E/I and total activity balance; spike-frequency adaptation for dynamic-range compression and nonlinear transfer; and metaplasticity to stabilize and regulate learning over multiple timescales. <cite id="9e942828-3">Homosynaptic and heterosynaptic plasticity jointly realize encoding and homeostasis</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-3">STDP and frequency/sequence dependence are broadly reported across excitatory and inhibitory synapses</cite>. <cite id="1f36c3b4-1">Adaptation-aware STDP achieves near-optimal transmission and matches in vivo theta dynamics</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-0">Metaplasticity provides a universal stabilizer of learned statistics through history-dependent induction thresholds</cite>.

Summary
- Universally operating learning mechanisms in biological neurons encompass: activity-correlation–based homosynaptic plasticity and spike-timing–dependent plasticity; spike-rate–dependent forms that integrate frequency and history; homeostatic synaptic scaling and heterosynaptic mechanisms that maintain excitation/inhibition and firing-rate balance; spike-frequency adaptation that tunes transfer functions to input statistics; and metaplasticity that conditions plasticity on past history and timescales. <cite id="9e942828-0">Metaplasticity stabilizes learned statistics and can be implemented via activity-dependent thresholds</cite>. <cite id="9e942828-1">These mechanisms are shaped by location, neuromodulators, and timescales, with homeostatic processes on slower timescales</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-2">Even the temporal window for STDP can be broad in adult human synapses</cite>. <cite id="1f36c3b4-0">Adaptation and STDP cooperate to optimize information transmission in sensory neurons</cite>. <cite id="d2c67462-4">Inhibitory microcircuits and oscillatory context provide universal scaffolds that shape plasticity expression across brain areas</cite>. Together, these mechanisms provide a coherent, cross-neuronal basis for learning while remaining flexible and system-specific in their details. </answer>

Title: Spike Timing Dependent Plasticity: A Consequence of More Fundamental Learning Rules
Snippet: For both Hebbian rate-based learning rules and linear STDPbased rules, runaway synaptic plasticity can occur (Bienenstock et al., 1982;Oja, 1982). The problem is not solved by imposing upper and lower bounds on synaptic weights, since synaptic weights can still saturate, leading to nonselective cells that respond equally to many input patterns. This problem of linear STDP models is associated with causality, which tends to result in presynaptic neurons firing slightly before postsynaptic neurons, and thus producing LTP. Therefore, synaptic saturation observed in linear STDP can be addressed by using an STDP kernel with slightly more LTD than LTP (Kempter et al., 1999;Song et al., 2000). 

Mechanistic models, which try to account for system level phenomena, like rate-based models, require stabilization mechanisms (Yeung et al., 2004;Yu et al., 2008;Clopath et al., 2010). It has been suggested that synaptic scaling (Turrigiano et al., 1998) might result in overall homeostatic change that reduces change in total synaptic strength on a neuron, which can prevent runaway plasticity. 

Such stabilization mechanisms seem related to metaplasticity observed experimentally (Abraham and Bear, 1996). Metaplasticity is at times used as a catch-all term for changes in learning rule. It is feasible that metaplasticity and synaptic scaling (Yeung et al., 2004) may arise naturally from cellular mechanisms that have a stabilizing influence. Synaptic plasticity models should therefore incorporate biophysical implementations of stabilization mechanisms for comparison to experiment.

This is achieved by a variety of homeostatic mechanisms operating at multiple nested levels, such as maintenance of excitation/inhibition balance and total activity at the network level, or homeostasis of synaptic weights at the single-cell level (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996;Haydon, 2001;Burrone and Murthy, 2003;Turrigiano, 2011;Davis, 2013). We ask: which forms of plasticity bring synaptic weights out of balance and which forms may serve to restore their balance?

The multitude of forms of synaptic plasticity can be segregated into three broad types, distinguished by the differential activity patterns required for their induction, distinct functions served in learning systems, and diverse computational roles. The first, homosynaptic plasticity, requires presynaptic activation of the synapse for the induction. By definition, it occurs only at synapses that were directly involved in activation of a cell during the induction, for example during afferent tetanization or pairing procedure ( Figure 1A). This form of plasticity is also called input specific, and, if the induction follows Hebbian-type learning rules, associative (Bliss and Collingridge, 1993). For induction of associative plasticity correlated activity of pre and postsynaptic neurons is crucial. Snippet: Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity (STDP) represents a fundamental mechanism of synaptic modification in the brain, characterized as a temporally asymmetric form of Hebbian learning. This process precisely adjusts the strength of connections between neurons based on the relative timing of their electrical impulses, known as action potentials or spikes [1,2]. This intricate timing-dependent modulation is widely regarded as a cornerstone for how the brain acquires and retains information, as well as how its complex neuronal circuits undergo development and refinement throughout an organism's lifespan [3]. 

In the canonical formulation, the update kernel depends on the spike timing difference ∆t = t post − t pre : 

where A + , A − > 0 are the maximal potentiation and depression amplitudes, and τ + , τ − are decay time constants. Small positive ∆t (presynaptic before postsynaptic) is interpreted as causal, producing strong potentiation; small negative ∆t (postsynaptic before presynaptic) is interpreted as anti-causal, producing strong depression. This yields an asymmetric, causality-driven plasticity window. 

The core principle of STDP dictates that if a presynaptic neuron fires its spike a few milliseconds before a postsynaptic neuron generates its own action potential, the synaptic connection between them typically undergoes Long-Term Potentiation (LTP), signifying a strengthening of that connection. Conversely, if the presynaptic spike arrives after the postsynaptic spike, the same synapse experiences Long-Term Depression (LTD), leading to its weakening [1]. This specific temporal window, often termed the STDP function or learning window, is not universal but can exhibit variations across different types of synapses, reflecting the diverse computational roles of various brain regions. 

The precise detection of these millisecond-scale spike timings is often mediated by NMDA receptors, which function as critical coincidence detectors within the synaptic machinery [4]. 

In computational models, STDP has been employed for unsupervised learning of visual and auditory patterns. For instance, Masquelier and Thorpe [5] demonstrated that spike-timing-based plasticity could be used to extract visual features from natural image sequences.

Snippet: Timing of the activation of presynaptic and postsynaptic cells plays a pivotal role in synaptic plasticity [66,67]. Spike timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) is considered a biologically plausible model for synaptic modifications occurring in vivo [68,69] and its occurrence has been reported in several brain regions, such as the corticostriatal pathway [70][71][72], the barrel cortex [73,74] and the visual cortex [75,76]. It is determined by the temporal order of action potential initiations and the narrow time between subsequent action potentials. In general, activation of the presynaptic cell immediately before activation of the postsynaptic cell leads to timing-dependent LTP, while activating the presynaptic neuron immediately after the postsynaptic cell elicits timing-dependent LTD [68,69]. The time window between these activations needs to be in the order of milliseconds, is specific for each synapse and depends on receptor kinetics, current densities and the release of retrograde messengers such as endocannabinoids [69]. Spontaneous spiking as well as changes in the spike frequency can further modulate the strength of plasticity, e.g. higher frequency stimulation has been described to increase the effect of timing-dependent LTP [69]. STDP was observed in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons and could be further modified by cholinergic, dopaminergic and adrenergic signaling [68], enabling prospective pharmacological modulation. It offers an alternative to frequency-dependent stimulation in clinical settings and has already been deployed in human studies to successfully modulate the force of the long-latency stretch reflex in healthy volunteers [77], while overall lower limb motor output was improved in patients with spinal cord injury [78].

Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity (STDP) represents a fundamental mechanism of synaptic modification in the brain, characterized as a temporally asymmetric form of Hebbian learning. This process precisely adjusts the strength of connections between neurons based on the relative timing of their electrical impulses, known as action potentials or spikes [1,2]. This intricate timing-dependent modulation is widely regarded as a cornerstone for how the brain acquires and retains information, as well as how its complex neuronal circuits undergo development and refinement throughout an organism's lifespan [3]. 

In the canonical formulation, the update kernel depends on the spike timing difference ∆t = t post − t pre : 

where A + , A − > 0 are the maximal potentiation and depression amplitudes, and τ + , τ − are decay time constants. Small positive ∆t (presynaptic before postsynaptic) is interpreted as causal, producing strong potentiation; small negative ∆t (postsynaptic before presynaptic) is interpreted as anti-causal, producing strong depression. This yields an asymmetric, causality-driven plasticity window. 

The core principle of STDP dictates that if a presynaptic neuron fires its spike a few milliseconds before a postsynaptic neuron generates its own action potential, the synaptic connection between them typically undergoes Long-Term Potentiation (LTP), signifying a strengthening of that connection. Conversely, if the presynaptic spike arrives after the postsynaptic spike, the same synapse experiences Long-Term Depression (LTD), leading to its weakening [1]. This specific temporal window, often termed the STDP function or learning window, is not universal but can exhibit variations across different types of synapses, reflecting the diverse computational roles of various brain regions. 

The precise detection of these millisecond-scale spike timings is often mediated by NMDA receptors, which function as critical coincidence detectors within the synaptic machinery [4].

Title: STDP in Adaptive Neurons Gives Close-To-Optimal Information Transmission
Snippet: Spike-frequency adaptation is known to enhance the transmission of information in sensory spiking neurons by rescaling the dynamic range for input processing, matching it to the temporal statistics of the sensory stimulus. Achieving maximal information transmission has also been recently postulated as a role for spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). However, the link between optimal plasticity and STDP in cortex remains loose, as does the relationship between STDP and adaptation processes. We investigate how STDP, as described by recent minimal models derived from experimental data, influences the quality of information transmission in an adapting neuron. We show that a phenomenological model based on triplets of spikes yields almost the same information rate as an optimal model specially designed to this end. In contrast, the standard pair-based model of STDP does not improve information transmission as much. This result holds not only for additive STDP with hard weight bounds, known to produce bimodal distributions of synaptic weights, but also for weight-dependent STDP in the context of unimodal but skewed weight distributions. Title: Hebbian Imprinting and Retrieval in Oscillatory Neural Networks
Snippet: We introduce a model of generalized Hebbian learning and retrieval in oscillatory neural networks modeling cortical areas such as hippocampus and olfactory cortex. Recent experiments have shown that synaptic plasticity depends on spike timing, especially on synapses from excitatory pyramidal cells, in hippocampus, and in sensory and cerebellar cortex. Learning is assumed to occur in a phase of neural plasticity, in which the network is clamped to external teaching signals. documents.snippet: We investigated the origin of spike frequency adaptation within a layered sensory network: the auditory pathway of locusts. Spike frequency adaptation as observed in an individual neuron may arise because of intrinsic or presynaptic adaptation mechanisms. To separate the contribution of different mechanisms, we recorded from the same cell during acoustic and intracellular current stimulation. By comparing current and acoustic stimulation, three distinct patterns of the distribution of adaptation mechanisms within the sensory network emerged: (1) balanced influence of both intrinsic and presynaptic adaptation mechanisms in an interneuron that summates over several receptor afferents (TN1), (2) predominantly inhibiting input as the source for spike frequency adaptation in a cell that transmits both pattern representation and directional information (BSN1), (3) primarily intrinsic, spike-triggered adaptation currents within an interneuron coding exclusively for direction (AN2). The time courses of spike frequency adaptation differed significantly between the cells types. Using the adaptation time constants, we were able to predict signal transmission properties for the different cells. We conclude that the adaptation mechanisms differ greatly among interneurons within this sensory pathway and are a function of their role in information processing.

documents.title: Hebbian Imprinting and Retrieval in Oscillatory Neural Networks
documents.snippet: We introduce a model of generalized Hebbian learning and retrieval in oscillatory neural networks modeling cortical areas such as hippocampus and olfactory cortex. Recent experiments have shown that synaptic plasticity depends on spike timing, especially on synapses from excitatory pyramidal cells, in hippocampus, and in sensory and cerebellar cortex. Here we study how such plasticity can be used to form memories and input representations when the neural dynamics are oscillatory, as is common in the brain (particularly in the hippocampus and olfactory cortex). Learning is assumed to occur in a phase of neural plasticity, in which the network is clamped to external teaching signals. By suitable manipulation of the nonlinearity of the neurons or the oscillation frequencies during learning, the model can be made, in a retrieval phase, either to categorize new inputs or to map them, in a continuous fashion, onto the space spanned by the imprinted patterns. We identify the first of these possibilities with the function of olfactory cortex and the second with the observed response characteristics of place cells in hippocampus. We investigate both kinds of networks analytically and by computer simulations, and we link the models with experimental findings, exploring, in particular, how the spike timing dependence of the synaptic plasticity constrains the computational function of the network and vice versa.
